summary: Describes how OpenPGP can provide privacy and authentication using the MIME security content types from RFC 1847.

plainLanguage.summary:
RFC 3156 says how to sign and encrypt an email with OpenPGP without breaking the email itself. A signed message is a MIME multipart with two parts: the text you wrote, and the signature beside it. An encrypted message has the control information in one part and the encrypted text in another.

Because mail gateways often rewrite a message on the way through, the document sets strict rules about how the signed text has to be encoded. If those rules are followed, the signature still checks out when the message arrives.

questions: how to sign and encrypt email with pgp
how does openpgp work with mime email
subtitle: How OpenPGP signing and encryption fit inside a MIME email message.

tldr.problem: Earlier work on running PGP inside MIME used a single application/pgp content type, and a receiver could not get at a signed message body without parsing PGP-specific data structures. RFC 2015 fixed this by moving to the security multiparts of RFC 1847, but the fit with the OpenPGP work was never finished.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3156 revises RFC 2015 and defines three media types. Signed mail is a multipart/signed object with the signature in its own part, encrypted mail is a multipart/encrypted object with a control part and an encrypted part, and public keys travel as application/pgp-keys.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Proposed Standard from August 2001 that updates RFC 2015 and has not itself been obsoleted or updated. It also lays down rules that keep a signature valid across mail gateways that re-encode a message.

facts.label: micalg values
facts.value: pgp-md5, pgp-sha1, pgp-ripemd160, pgp-md2, pgp-tiger192, pgp-haval-5-160

today: RFC 3156 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2001. It updates RFC 2015, which had used the withdrawn application/pgp content type, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The three media types it registers are the ones the document defines.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Work on integrating PGP with MIME, including the since withdrawn application/pgp content type, prior to RFC 2015 suffered from a number of problems, the most significant of which was the inability to recover signed message bodies without parsing data structures specific to PGP. RFC 2015 makes use of the solution proposed in RFC 1847, which defines security multipart formats for MIME. The security multiparts clearly separate the signed message body from the signature, and have a number of other desirable properties. This document revises RFC 2015 to adopt the integration of PGP and MIME to the needs which emerged during the work on the OpenPGP specification.

The document defines three content types for implementing security and privacy with OpenPGP: application/pgp-encrypted, application/pgp-signature and application/pgp-keys.
sections.plainLanguage: The old approach wrapped the whole message in one PGP blob, which meant a mail program had to understand PGP to find the text. The security multiparts put the text and the signature in separate parts of a normal MIME message, so any mail program can find the text and a PGP program can find the signature.

sections.title: OpenPGP Data Formats and Transfer Encoding
sections.content:
OpenPGP implementations can generate either ASCII armor or 8-bit binary output when encrypting data, generating a digital signature, or extracting public key data. The ASCII armor output is the required method for data transfer. This allows users who do not have the means to interpret the formats described in the document to extract and use the OpenPGP information in the message. When the amount of data to be transmitted requires that it be sent in many parts, the MIME message/partial mechanism should be used rather than the multi-part ASCII armor OpenPGP format.

Multipart/signed and multipart/encrypted are to be treated by agents as opaque, meaning that the data is not to be altered in any way. However, many existing mail gateways will detect if the next hop does not support MIME or 8-bit data and perform conversion to either Quoted-Printable or Base64. This presents serious problems for multipart/signed, in particular, where the signature is invalidated when such an operation occurs. For this reason all data signed according to this protocol must be constrained to 7 bits, and 8-bit data must be encoded using either Quoted-Printable or Base64. This also includes the case where a signed object is also encrypted. The restriction increases the likelihood that the signature will be valid upon receipt.

Implementations must also make sure that no trailing whitespace is present after the MIME encoding has been applied. In most cases trailing whitespace can be removed or protected by applying an appropriate content-transfer-encoding. Special care must be taken when any header lines, either in MIME entity headers or in embedded RFC 822 headers, are present which only consist of whitespace: such lines must be removed entirely, since replacing them by empty lines would turn them into header delimiters and change the semantics of the message. The restrictions on whitespace are necessary in order to make the hash calculated invariant under the text and binary mode signature mechanisms provided by OpenPGP, and they help to avoid compatibility problems with PGP implementations which predate the OpenPGP specification.

If any line begins with the string From , it is strongly suggested that either Quoted-Printable or Base64 MIME encoding be applied. If Quoted-Printable is used, at least one of the characters in the string should be encoded using the hexadecimal coding rule, because many mail transfer and delivery agents treat From as the start of a new message and insert a right angle bracket in front of any line beginning with it, which invalidates the signature.

Data that is only to be encrypted is allowed to contain 8-bit characters and trailing whitespace and therefore need not undergo the conversion to a 7-bit format, nor the stripping of whitespace. The document's implementor's note is that applications should be conservative in what they generate and liberal in what they accept: it would be wise for an implementation to accept messages with any content-transfer-encoding, but restrict generation to the 7-bit format required by the memo, so that future compatibility is possible in the event the internet SMTP framework becomes 8-bit friendly.
sections.plainLanguage: Two rules do most of the work. Signed text must be reduced to 7 bits, using Quoted-Printable or Base64 if needed, so that a gateway which re-encodes the message does not break the signature. And trailing whitespace must be removed, because some mail programs silently change it and others add a bracket to lines starting with From .

sections.title: OpenPGP Encrypted Data
sections.content:
Before OpenPGP encryption, the data is written in MIME canonical format, with body and headers. OpenPGP encrypted data is denoted by the multipart/encrypted content type, and must have a protocol parameter value of application/pgp-encrypted. The value of the parameter must be enclosed in quotes.

The multipart/encrypted MIME body must consist of exactly two body parts. The first has content type application/pgp-encrypted and contains the control information. A message complying with the standard must contain a Version: 1 field in this body. Since the OpenPGP packet format contains all other information necessary for decrypting, no other information is required here. The second MIME body part must contain the actual encrypted data and must be labeled with a content type of application/octet-stream.
sections.plainLanguage: An encrypted message has exactly two parts. The first is a small control part holding one line, Version: 1. The second holds the encrypted bytes. Everything else needed to decrypt is inside the OpenPGP data itself.

sections.title: OpenPGP Signed Data
sections.content:
OpenPGP signed messages are denoted by the multipart/signed content type, with a protocol parameter which must have the value application/pgp-signature and must be quoted.

The micalg parameter for the application/pgp-signature protocol must contain exactly one hash symbol of the format pgp-<hash-identifier>, where the identifier names the Message Integrity Check algorithm used to generate the signature. Hash symbols are constructed from the text names registered in the OpenPGP message format, by converting the text name to lower case and prefixing it with the four characters pgp-. The currently defined values are pgp-md5, pgp-sha1, pgp-ripemd160, pgp-md2, pgp-tiger192 and pgp-haval-5-160.

The multipart/signed body must consist of exactly two parts. The first contains the signed data in MIME canonical format, including a set of appropriate content headers describing the data. The second body must contain the OpenPGP digital signature, and must be labeled with a content type of application/pgp-signature.

When the OpenPGP digital signature is generated, the data to be signed must first be converted to its content-type specific canonical form; for text/plain this means conversion to an appropriate character set and conversion of line endings to the canonical CR LF sequence. An appropriate content-transfer-encoding is then applied, and line endings in the encoded data must use the canonical CR LF sequence where appropriate, though the canonical line ending may or may not be present on the last line of encoded data and must not be included in the signature if absent. MIME content headers are then added to the body, each ending with the canonical CR LF sequence. Any trailing whitespace must then be removed from the signed material. The digital signature must be calculated over both the data to be signed and its set of content headers. Finally, the signature must be generated detached from the signed data so that the process does not alter the signed data in any way.

Upon receipt of a signed message, an application must convert line endings to the canonical CR LF sequence before the signature can be verified, because the local mail transfer agent may have converted them to a local end of line convention. It must then pass both the signed data and its associated content headers, along with the OpenPGP signature, to the signature verification service.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing happens in a fixed order so that a sender and a receiver compute the same hash. The text is put in canonical form, encoded, given its headers, stripped of trailing whitespace, and then signed together with those headers. The signature is kept separate so that nothing can change the text on its way to being signed.

sections.title: Encrypted and Signed Data
sections.content:
Sometimes it is desirable to both digitally sign and then encrypt a message. The protocol allows two methods of accomplishing this.

Under RFC 1847 encapsulation, the data is first signed as a multipart/signed body, and then encrypted to form the final multipart/encrypted body. This is most useful for standard MIME-compliant message forwarding.

Under the combined method, the OpenPGP packet format describes a method for signing and encrypting data in a single OpenPGP message. This method is allowed in order to reduce processing overhead and increase compatibility with non-MIME implementations of OpenPGP. The resulting data is formatted as a multipart/encrypted object as described earlier.

Messages which are encrypted and signed in the combined fashion are required to follow the same canonicalization rules as multipart/signed objects. It is explicitly allowed for an agent to decrypt a combined message and rewrite it as a multipart/signed object using the signature data embedded in the encrypted version.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to sign and encrypt together. Sign first and encrypt the result, which suits mail systems that forward ordinary MIME messages. Or do both inside one OpenPGP message, which costs less work and also works for programs that do not speak MIME at all.

sections.title: Distribution of OpenPGP Public Keys
sections.content: The content type is application/pgp-keys, with no required parameters and no optional parameters. A MIME body part of this content type contains ASCII-armored transferable public key packets as defined in the OpenPGP message format.
sections.plainLanguage: Public keys travel as their own MIME part, armored so that they survive being passed through text-only systems.

sections.title: Media Type Registrations
sections.content: The document defines three media types. The application/pgp-encrypted type has no required or optional parameters, currently always consists of a single 7-bit text string, has no magic number, no file extension and no Macintosh file type code, and is intended for common usage. The application/pgp-signature type has no required or optional parameters, its content always consists of 7-bit text, it has no magic number, file extensions asc and sig, and Macintosh file type code pgDS. The application/pgp-keys type has no required or optional parameters, its content always consists of 7-bit text, it has no magic number, file extension asc, and no Macintosh file type code. The author and change controller for all three is Michael Elkins.
sections.plainLanguage: Three registrations, all with the same shape: no parameters, 7-bit text, and no security or interoperability caveats of their own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Signatures of a canonical text document as defined in the OpenPGP message format ignore trailing white space in signed material. Implementations which choose to use signatures of canonical text documents will therefore not be able to detect the addition of whitespace in transit. The security considerations of the underlying protocols are covered in RFC 2046 and RFC 1848.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one gap. A signature over a canonical text document does not notice trailing whitespace, so an attacker who adds whitespace in transit leaves the signature valid. The document points at RFC 2046 and RFC 1848 for the wider picture.

children.label: text/plain
children.note: The signed data in MIME canonical form, with its content headers.

viz.caption: The six steps to build a signature

items.title: Canonicalise
items.text: Convert the data to be signed to its content-type specific canonical form. For text/plain that means the right character set and canonical CR LF line endings.

items.title: Apply the transfer encoding
items.text: Use a content-transfer-encoding, with canonical CR LF line endings where appropriate. A canonical line ending on the last line must not be included in the signature if absent.

items.title: Add the content headers
items.text: Add the MIME content headers to the body, each ending with the canonical CR LF sequence.

items.title: Strip trailing whitespace
items.text: Remove any trailing whitespace from the signed material.

items.title: Sign data and headers together
items.text: Calculate the digital signature over both the data to be signed and its set of content headers.

items.title: Detach the signature
items.text: Generate the signature detached from the signed data, so that the process does not alter the signed data in any way.

items.label: Encrypted control part
items.desc: Always a single 7-bit text string. No magic number, no file extension and no Macintosh file type code.

items.label: The signature part
items.desc: Always 7-bit text. File extensions asc and sig, Macintosh file type code pgDS.

items.label: The public key part
items.desc: Always 7-bit text. File extension asc, no Macintosh file type code.
